items.title: FHFA set to order Fannie, Freddie to accept two-bureau credit reports
items.description: The Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) plans to direct Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to shift from “tri-merge” to “bi-merge” reports for loan deliveries within weeks, a person familiar with the plans told Bloomberg. FHFA officials did not immediately respond to HousingWire ’s request for comment. The change, which would alter a core element of mortgage underwriting for loans sold to the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs), could be announced by FHFA Director Bill Pulte during the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) conference in Chicago on Oct. 12, Bloomberg reported. A bi-merge option was on the table during the Biden administration when the FHFA was run by Sandra Thompson, but the plan was delayed due to implementation challenges. Recently, some players in the industry have defended the use of a single-file option , with the MBA being the most vocal supporter of the idea. In early September, Pulte took to social media to say the FHFA was “seriously considering” the adoption of a bi-merge credit report. “ Equifax , Experian , and TransUnion have been overcharging Americans for far too long. This will end soon. We are seriously considering bi-merge, and stronger solutions (SAFER and SOUNDER). We will not allow companies to take advantage of American consumers. No more,” Pulte wrote on social media on Thursday. A tri-merge credit report combines data from the three bureaus. Under the new policy, lenders would be able to pick only two of them. The requirement is expected to take effect one to three months after it is announced, per Bloomberg. The latest move comes on the heels of Pulte’s decision to allow Fannie and Freddie to use credit scores from VantageScore , a joint venture of Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Earlier this week, Pulte said the GSEs would use a single pricing grid that treats VantageScore 4.0 scores as equivalent to Classic FICO scores, reversing earlier GSE grids released just weeks prior that assumed VantageScore overstated borrower creditworthiness by about 20 points versus FICO. Related More: Bill Pulte Credit Score Federal Housing Finance Agency

items.title: FHA nominee Matt Jones says he'll target more housing supply and lower costs
items.description: Matt Jones, President Donald Trump’s nominee to hold the dual role of assistant secretary for the Department Housing and Urban Development ( HUD ) and commissioner of the Federal Housing Administration ( FHA ), told senators he would focus on increased housing supply, lower costs and expanded access to homeownership. Jones, who previously worked as senior counsel for the Senate ’s banking and finance committee and now serves as HUD’s deputy assistant secretary for single-family housing, appeared before the same committee for a confirmation hearing on Thursday morning. In his opening statement, he described housing affordability as a defining challenge and said FHA-insured loans help more than 3,000 families buy homes each business day — most of them first-time buyers. In his testimony, Jones added that FHA had streamlined more than 150 program requirements, which he said reduced costs for consumers. He also pointed to manufactured housing as a way to increase supply, noting that HUD had showcased its first two-story manufactured home and described non-site-built housing as an opportunity to reduce construction costs and expand options for homebuyers. “Paired with the implementation of the 21st Century ROAD legislation , we are looking at a generational opportunity to accelerate the construction of non-site-built housing, reduce its cost and increase its appeal for the American people,” Jones said. His other stated priorities include finalizing guidance to bar large institutional investors from buying HUD-owned properties or participating in single-family note sales, and to begin accepting two additional credit-score models for FHA underwriting starting in 2027. Jones said the new models could help younger borrowers with limited credit histories qualify for mortgages. “This will benefit our insurance fund through improved predictive power, and will benefit responsible young consumers who have done everything right, made payments on time, but may not yet see those trends reflected under older models — not to mention this will create competitive pressure to continue to sharpen these models, while we hope to also bring down the cost of pulling a credit report,” he said. In response to questions from Sen. Mike Crapo (R-Idaho), Jones said FHA would continue cutting regulatory costs in home construction, mortgage origination and servicing. He also said the agency could support affordable multifamily development by coordinating FHA insurance with other public funding, including Low-Income Housing Tax Credits . Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) criticized the timing of the hearing, arguing that holding it during a Senate recess limited senators’ ability to provide oversight. “Committees almost never hold nomination hearings when the Senate has adjourned for recess. It is irresponsible to waive senior officials through the process without giving every senator the opportunity to ask questions and the American people the right to hear the answers,” she said. Warren also addressed Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte’s decision to allocate a “peer-matched” budget to its Office of Inspector General (OIG). “Pulte is unlawfully shutting down the work of the Inspector General, (who is) responsible for investigating misconduct at the Federal Housing Finance Agency and in multi-trillion-dollar mortgage markets. The Inspector General’s office alerted Congress that the cuts will effectively shut down their work,” Warren said. Industry support for Jones Industry trade groups have expressed support for Jones’ nomination. Ahead of Jones’s hearing Thursday morning, the Community Home Lenders of America ( CHLA ) said that it strongly supports his confirmation. In a letter addressed to the Senate banking committee, CHLA cited Jones’s housing policy expertise, government experience and mortgage industry knowledge . items.title: Mortgage Banking Summit: FHFA’s unified LLPA grid for FICO, VantageScore raises investor concerns
items.description: The Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA)’s decision to apply the same loan-level price adjustments (LLPAs) for Classic FICO and VantageScore 4.0 loans is being viewed as a de facto incentive for VantageScore adoption — and as a source of new uncertainty around investor reactions and risk-based pricing. Industry leaders at HousingWire ’s Mortgage Banking Summit in Dallas on Thursday said the move, which eliminates a prior 20-point calibration between the two credit scores, will likely accelerate use of VantageScore but leaves open questions on how mortgage-backed securities (MBS) investors will respond. “There’s some confusion about how that actually works; the immediate reaction we got from our members was this is going to take time to implement,” Bill Killmer , senior vice president for legislative and political affairs at the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), said on stage. On Monday, FHFA Director Bill Pulte said Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will move to a single pricing matrix for LLPAs, rather than maintaining separate grids for Classic FICO and VantageScore 4.0. Pulte said the change follows feedback from lenders and consumers, while arguing that separate grids “makes zero sense.” “Fannie and Freddie are hereby moving to ONE PRICING GRID with VantageScore joining the existing FICO Classic pricing grid,” Pulte posted on X . Previously, LLPAs calibrated for FICO were applied to VantageScore 4.0 at 20 points higher. The top purchase tier for FICO remained 780 and above, aligned with an 800-plus VantageScore bucket. With VantageScore 4.0 now mapping directly into the existing FICO grid, more borrowers will qualify for lower LLPAs when underwritten with VantageScore instead of FICO, without any change in underlying collateral or borrower profile, executives said. Killmer said there is “no question it will increase utilization of Vantage.” But the response by investors remains a key unknown, he added. “Is there going to be some bias in terms of their appetite for Vantage-driven MBS versus FICO?” Killmer asked. “Does that mean that FICO accelerates to put their 10T model out as opposed to Classic sooner than they might have?” Other participants at the conference also questioned whether investors will differentiate between MBS pools backed by loans underwritten with newer credit scoring models versus Classic FICO, especially if fee structures no longer explicitly compensate for the modeled risk differences. “What concerns me now that the LLPAs are the same is we just don’t have enough data to bank on it when it comes to secondary market,” said Greg Sher , managing director at NFM Lending . Erin Dee , senior vice president and chief information officer at BankSouth Mortgage , said her company will price loans backed by VS4 and Classic FICO on the front end, but those “buying my bonds on the back end are not going to do the same thing. … So what position is this going to put lenders in when the secondary market disagrees with the LLPA?” she asked. Early adoption So far, the monthly volume of VS4-backed loans remains limited but concentrated among the largest agency originators. VantageScore accounted for 5.5% of originations through Fannie and Freddie in September, flat compared to August, according to Keefe, Bruyette Woods (KBW) analysts. Rocket Mortgage and United Wholesale Mortgage were responsible for 95% of that VantageScore volume, with penetration of 34% at Rocket — which recently announced that VS4 is their default credit model — and 24.9% at UWM, the analysts said. The removal of the 20-point haircut on VantageScore 4.0 loans results “in a lower LLPA for a large percentage of loans if they use VS4 instead of FICO,” KBW analysts wrote. “We see the action to combine the grids as a backdoor LLPA reduction, since most VS4 borrowers will now have a lower LLPA.” For example, a borrower with a 700 FICO score and a 720 VantageScore would previously have been charged a 1

items.title: Eastham Capital sues Audubon over troubled Alabama property

Permission granted by Eastham Capital As more apartment deals run into trouble, the issues at the 408-unit Cadence at Bluff Park in Hoover, Alabama, stand out. In June 2021, entities related to Chamblee, Georgia-based apartment owner, manager and developer Audubon and Boca Raton, Florida-based investor Eastham Capital bought the property for $32.7 million in a deal that was covered by local news outlet AL.com. However, that wouldn’t be the last time the Cadence at Bluff Park appeared in local news stories. Although local media had already raised concerns, the property's alleged problems came to light in a July lawsuit filed in Delaware’s Court of Chancery. Eastham Capital Fund VI filed a lawsuit in July accusing Audubon founder and CEO Andrew Schwarz and his affiliates of badly mismanaging an apartment property in Alabama and breaching the terms of their agreement. As a limited partner, Eastham contributed $8.8 million to help buy Cadence at Bluff Park in March 2021. Over time, it made almost $3.8 million in additional capital contributions, bringing its total investment to almost $12.6 million, according to the lawsuit. Eastham claimed that the defendants could not achieve initial pro formas despite almost five years of owning the property and collecting nearly $1.4 million in fees. The filing also alleges that Schwarz and the Audubon entities racked up more than $104,000 in late fees for delinquent mortgage payments. The plaintiff is asking for indemnification for “any and all losses, damages, and liabilities,’” according to the suit. “The Property was a disaster and was clearly not being professionally managed,” according to an email attributed to a former property employee in the court filing. Audubon did not reply to emails from and could not be reached by phone by Multifamily Dive by publication time. But allegedly that was only the beginning of the problems. According to an email in the court filing, an anonymous former employee of Audubon claimed that units 813-815 were filled with sewage and water for six months, leading to the growth of mold and mushrooms. The culprit was “incompetent vendors who erroneously removed two support beams such that two buildings in the Property started sinking,” according to the anonymous emailer cited in court filings. The former employee also claimed that smoke detectors and fire extinguishers “were not reinstalled after the renovations” in the second quarter of 2025 and “dozens of units with mold as well as other health hazards and safety concerns which were not addressed by management,” according to the suit. items.title: Howard Hughes names Kaminski President of Arizona region
items.description: Howard Hughes Communities , the real estate platform of Howard Hughes Holdings Inc. , has promoted Kate Kaminski to president of its Arizona region, the company announced on Thursday. In the role, she will oversee strategy, investment, development and operations for Teravalis, a 37,000-acre, master-planned community in Buckeye, Arizona entitled for up to 113,000 homes. Kaminski succeeds longtime industry executive Charley Freericks in a planned leadership transition. Freericks, who has been leading the Arizona region and the early stages of Teravalis, will remain with Howard Hughes Communities as a senior advisor focused on long-range initiatives and new opportunities, according to the announcement. Kaminski joined Howard Hughes in 2024 as chief operating officer of the Arizona region. Working alongside Freericks, she has helped build out a local team, deepen technical capabilities and expand relationships across the Greater Phoenix business community. She was recently appointed to the Greater Phoenix Economic Council’s board of directors, connecting Howard Hughes with public- and private-sector leaders focused on business attraction and regional economic growth. “When we brought Charley and Kate to Howard Hughes Communities a few years ago, we had this transition in mind,” David O’Reilly, CEO of Howard Hughes, said in the announcement. “Charley has helped establish a strong foundation for Teravalis, and Kate has earned the opportunity to build on it.” The leadership change comes as Howard Hughes moves from early-stage planning and infrastructure at Teravalis into more active residential and future commercial development. The community is envisioned to include multiple residential villages, employment centers, commercial space, schools, services and amenities designed to support long-term population and job growth on the western edge of the Phoenix metro. Floreo, the first residential village at Teravalis, opened for home sales in late 2025 and is now welcoming residents. The village is planned for about 8,500 homes, with seven homebuilders currently active, according to the company. Ongoing infrastructure work and planning for future employment and commercial districts are intended to support the next phases of residential absorption and nonresidential demand. “Teravalis represents an extraordinary opportunity to build something the Phoenix MSA has never had at scale,” Kaminski said in the release. “As we welcome our first residents, our responsibility is to deliver on the promise of this community. That means planning for the homes, employment, schools, services and gathering places that support everyday life.” Kaminski brings more than two decades of executive experience in real estate investment, land development, corporate strategy, capital markets and operations. Before joining Howard Hughes, she spent nearly 20 years at Walton Global , ultimately serving as global chief operating officer, according to the announcement. That background aligns with the capital-intensive and staged nature of building out a large master planned community such as Teravalis. “Kate understands the business, cares about this team, and brings the perspective and energy to lead its next stage of growth,” Freericks said. Related More: Arizona homebuilder

items.title: High-Flying Midtown Office Market Back To Pre-Pandemic Health
items.description: High-Flying Midtown Office Market Back To Pre-Pandemic Health October 1, 2026 | 8:29 pm ET Ciara Long, New York City There was no summer slowdown for Manhattan's office market, where available space is rapidly dwindling, rents are soaring and Midtown has hit a key milestone. Unsplash/Luca Bravo The amount of available office space in Midtown fell to 27.7M SF by the end of the third quarter, matching the figure from March 2020, according to a new Colliers report. It's the first NYC submarket to recover all of the occupancy losses caused by the pandemic. More than 10M SF of leases were signed across the borough, keeping Manhattan's office market on pace for its most active year since 2000. The tightening market has allowed owners of Class-A buildings across the borough to push asking rents to an all-time high of $85.45 per SF, according to Colliers. “The Manhattan office market’s recovery continued at a rapid pace throughout the summer and into the early days of autumn,” Colliers Executive Managing Director of Research and Business Development Franklin Wallach said in a statement. Midtown’s availability rate dwindled to 11.9%, while its average asking rent is now $85.08 per SF, up 5.4% year-over-year — the fastest annual Q3 jump since 2014. Proskauer Rose signed the biggest deal of the quarter at 11 Times Square with its 478K SF expansion. “Rents are rising across the board,” SL Green Director of Leasing Steven Durels said at the Bank of America Global CEO Real Estate Conference last month. “They're not limited to just the high-end part of the market.” It was also a record-breaking period in the tech hub of Midtown South . Powered by Anthropic ’s bumper 466K SF full-building lease at 330 Hudson St., the 4.8M SF of leasing activity was the most for a third quarter on record, according to Colliers. Artificial intelligence firms took nearly 1.1M SF of Manhattan office space, continuing their expansion after taking 800K SF in Q2 and 790K SF in all of 2025. Downtown, by contrast, lost momentum last quarter, with 850K SF of leases signed — 21.7% below its quarterly average over the past five years. But that didn’t detract from Manhattan’s momentum: The overall availability rate shrank by 2.4% between July and October, ending the quarter at 12.4%, according to the brokerage’s data. The scramble for space has put the city’s office landlords firmly in the driver’s seat, with robust tenant demand and buildings being converted to apartments putting an end to the yearslong rise in tenant concessions . “As we enter the final quarter of the year, the market is beginning a new chapter after achieving several critical recovery milestones,” Wallach said. items.title: Lenders Warn Commercial Real Estate's 'Day Of Reckoning' Is Close At Hand
items.description: Lenders Warn Commercial Real Estate's 'Day Of Reckoning' Is Close At Hand October 1, 2026 | 4:06 pm ET Sasha Jones, New York City Soaring 10-year Treasury yields have thrown ice-cold water on CRE’s typically unrelenting optimism. The key economic benchmark hit 5.3% on Wednesday afternoon, reaching its highest level since 2002 at the end of its biggest quarterly increase since 1994 . As the 10-year climbed, some of the industry’s largest players — already battered by high construction costs , inflation and geopolitical upheaval — watched the historic upswing from Bisnow ’s National Commercial Real Estate Finance Event and agreed that times were about to get a lot tougher. “The volatility is the worst thing for all of us,” AEW Capital Management Chief Operating Officer Lauren O’Neil said onstage. “When you have rates jump 75 basis points in a matter of 30 days, that just puts a complete chill out on the market.” Unsplash/Andrew Dawes The rapid run-up has forced the real estate industry to realize that deals that worked a month ago may not pencil out tomorrow. As lenders pump the brakes, a stalemate risks jeopardizing the recovery that investors have long been betting on. “For a long time, legacy owners have had the perspective that things have moved against me, and I'm waiting for them to move back in my favor before I do anything,” Dansker Capital Group CEO Andrew Dansker said. “That perspective is changing, and I think that is going to cause owners to make different choices and make their lenders make different choices.” The investors and lenders at the event said real estate values are likely to come down because of the higher rates, creating buying opportunities. “It will be painful for some legacy operators who got wiped out,” Dansker added. “But it will ultimately be positive for everyone in terms of resetting basis.” Bisnow/Ciara Long Windels Marx Lane Mittendorf’s Jack Conboy, KBS’s Sondra Wenger, AEW Capital Management’s Lauren O'Neil, Forvis Mazars’ John Confrey, KeyBank Real Estate Capital’s Joshua Mayers and Poverni Sheikh Group’s Eugene Poverni The 10-year yield dipped below 4% on Feb. 27, one day before the U.S. launched its attack on Iran , and it has been on a growth path ever since. It closed that day at 3.96% — its low for the year — and has not fallen below 4% since then. Yields first cleared 4.5% in May. Right before the Federal Open Market Committee ’s September meeting, the benchmark pushed past 5% , considered a key psychological threshold. “Economists have this great concept called ceteris paribus. It means all else being equal,” KeyBank Real Estate Capital Senior Banker Joshua Mayers said. “The trouble is, the real world doesn't work like that. We're running multiple weird, crazy experiments all over the place right now, and it's really challenging.” Rising oil prices and an ongoing trade war have fueled inflation fears, prompting the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates . At the same time, the economy and labor market have remained surprisingly resilient . Strong corporate growth, particularly among artificial intelligence companies, has kept stocks attractive to investors even as Treasury yields climb. Meanwhile, the national debt surpassed a record $40T in August, adding to concerns about the government’s enormous borrowing needs and putting further pressure on long-term Treasury yields. The world is an investor’s oyster, but for CRE, that means the competition for capital is getting tougher, borrowing costs are up, and property values are feeling the squeeze. “I just think we’ve been the bad word, the bad sector for a long time, and any uncertainty makes it a little bit harder to raise capital,” said Nailah Flake, a managing director at Brookfield who leads its real estate credit arm. items.title: IQHQ Lands $245M Loan From Cannabis REIT For Cambridge Lab Campus
items.description: IQHQ Lands $245M Loan From Cannabis REIT For Cambridge Lab Campus October 1, 2026 | 4:39 pm ET Taylor Driscoll, Boston Innovative Industrial Properties , an investor that previously focused on cannabis real estate before breaking into life sciences last year, is now providing a big loan to a lab campus in Cambridge's Alewife neighborhood. Google Earth IQHQ's Alewife Park District in 2024 The San Diego-based cannabis REIT entered into an agreement to provide a $245M mezzanine loan to IQHQ for the first phase of its 27-acre Alewife Park campus, IIP announced Thursday . The loan will help pay off an existing $85M bridge loan and will fund the completion of the project and its lease-up. Roughly $111M will be provided at closing, with the remaining $134M funded over time through late next year. The loan is expected to yield a 15.8% interest rate, IIP said, and has a February 2028 maturity date with a one-year extension option. IQHQ had already invested $800M in the project prior to IIP's loan, according to the developer. The development's first phase consists of three buildings totaling 392K SF. It is already 78% leased to Lila Therapeutics, which signed a 235K SF lease at 1 and 5 Alewife Park last year. Its second phase is planned for two other sites with up to 364K SF of development potential. The developer acquired the Alewife property in 2020 for $125M . IIP, founded in 2016, has primarily focused on investing in cannabis-related real estate. The company was co-founded by a veteran of the life sciences real estate sector, Alan Gold , who also co-founded Alexandria Real Estate Equities and served as CEO of BioMed Realty Trust . In August 2025, IIP struck its first deal in the life sciences sector , also with IQHQ. It funded a $100M revolving line of credit for the life sciences developer and committed to purchasing $170M in preferred stock. “We are pleased to further expand our life science portfolio through this investment for Alewife Park, which we believe will provide attractive risk-adjusted returns for IIP shareholders and significant accretion to our earnings,” Gold, IIP's executive chairman, said in a statement. IQHQ faced some hurdles amid the life sciences sector's slowdown. The developer halted its $1B Fenway Center project in Boston and was sued by Aimco over a soured $50M investment into a multifamily component of a new development. Its Alewife project is located near the site of an even larger development planned by Healthpeak Properties. The firm last month received Cambridge Planning Board approval for the permits needed to begin its 5M SF Alewife Quadrangle project, with more than 2,300 housing units and 2.6M SF of office and lab space. items.title: Why Brookfield Residential put data governance ahead of AI
items.description: Editor’s note: This installment of Built for This is part of HousingWire’s ongoing examination of homebuilding leaders and companies improving their businesses in a housing market that offers little outside help. Brookfield Residential CIO Brandon Sharp will take the stage at the HousingWire Homebuilder Summit , Oct. 19–21 in Dallas. When Brandon Sharp applied for a job to join the ranks of homebuilders in 2003, he had no homebuilding experience. Sharp, now Chief Information Officer at Brookfield Residential , was interviewing for a controller job with Standard Pacific in Austin. The division president wanted somebody who knew the business. Sharp flexed into explaining why he should hire somebody who didn’t. He answered without missing a beat. “Because I am going to own the data more than anyone has ever owned the data,” Sharp recalls telling him. He got the job, and 23 years later, Sharp describes what followed as a rigorous education in how difficult keeping that promise actually is. “This stuff is hard,” he says. “It is genuinely, notoriously hard.” Despite enormous investments in enterprise software, reporting systems, and business intelligence, Sharp, now an advanced student in the field of interoperable systems, says a genuine single source of truth still eludes many large homebuilders. Homebuilding companies and their business and operational partners are all driving toward artificial intelligence and its dividends. That elusive promise of a single source of [data] truth remains table stakes in the rules of the game. AI promises faster analysis, better forecasting, more productive employees and the ability to find relationships among enormous amounts of information. Yet the quality of any of those outputs ultimately depends on something considerably less exciting: whether the information flowing through the business can be trusted in the first place. Brookfield Residential has spent much of the past eight years working on solutions to that challenge. The result offers an important lesson for builders facing a difficult market while also trying to prepare their organizations for a technology transition that is moving faster than most can comfortably absorb. Before an organization can become much smarter with AI, it may first have to become considerably better at making sound decisions about the basics. The hard work underarching the technology Sharp frames successful data transformation around three non-negotiable enterprise commitments, each requiring time and day-to-day focus: conviction, clarity and capital. Conviction means leadership genuinely believes the work matters enough to continue when it gets difficult. Clarity means people understand where the organization is going, why it is going there, and what it will require of them. Capital includes the obvious financial investment. Sharp also emphasizes another scarce resource: the time and heads-down resolve of team members who still have homes to sell, trades to manage, and customers to serve while the transformation is underway. Brookfield brought each of the three commitments together in a binding alignment, integration, adoption and implementation of operational initiatives. Beginning in 2018 and continuing through the pandemic, the company set off on a company-wide transformation that included an ERP, a common unified data schema, an enterprise data warehouse and a series of reporting systems. Sharp estimates that Brookfield invested more than 250,000 internal hours across 20 business groups and implemented seven major business systems, much of it while employees were working remotely during COVID. Software can be purchased. Organizational capability cannot Brookfield’s investment would have been for naught without determined buy-in from finance professionals, operators, division presidents, and regional leaders who participated in work that could easily have been dismissed or at least relegated to a lower priority as an IT initiative. items.title: Mamdani Officials, RGB Members Had Frequent Contact Before Rent Freeze, Communications Reveal
items.description: Mamdani Officials, RGB Members Had Frequent Contact Before Rent Freeze, Communications Reveal October 1, 2026 | 4:15 pm ET Sasha Jones, New York City The Rent Guidelines Board’s leadership repeatedly communicated with Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s office in the months leading up to June's vote to freeze rents on the city's stabilized apartments, according to texts and emails filed as evidence in court on Thursday. Bisnow/Sasha Jones Tenant advocates protest outside of El Museo del Barrio before the Rent Guidelines Board's 2026 vote. The communications include a draft of the RGB’s explanatory statement, sent by RGB Chair Chantella Mitchell to Deputy Chief of Staff to the Deputy Mayor for Housing Arvind Sindhwani, on June 16, more than a week before the official vote. The initial batch of produced communications was filed in court on the same day that rents were frozen on more than 1 million New York City apartments. Landlords have contested the unprecedented 0% increase on one- and two-year leases, claiming that the independent board’s process was illegally influenced by the mayor. “It is standard for the RGB to communicate as needed with other government entities, including the Mayor’s Office, subject matter experts, and other stakeholders,” Matt Rauschenbach, a spokesperson for the mayor, said in a statement. “This year, communications were limited, non-substantive, and in no way reflect any attempts to influence the outcome of the vote.” A four-year rent freeze was a central campaign promise by Mamdani. Though the mayor appoints board members, the nine-person body is supposed to base its decision solely on the data and testimony provided by researchers, advocates, landlords and tenants. The information is presented in public hearings over several months leading up to the vote. Last week, Richmond County Supreme Court Judge Brendan Lantry ordered more than two dozen top city officials and RGB members to turn over their phones and emails for inspection. In a letter to the judge, the city’s top attorney, Steven Banks, wrote that there is “absolutely no merit” to the accusations and that the process was conducted with the “utmost honesty, integrity, and independence.” There were 101 emails between Mitchell and Sindhwani, who Banks said is the “designated point of contact at City Hall for logistical and liaison matters related to the RGB in the current administration.” He pointed out that in 2025, there were 228 emails between then-RGB Chair Doug Apple and then-Mayor Eric Adams' City Hall point of contact. But the plaintiff’s attorneys, which consist of a team from Rosenberg Estis and Dechert co-chair Randy Mastro — who served as deputy mayor under Adams — said the search produced nearly 1,000 documents in total, spanning 3,000 pages. “What our review of this initial production has revealed, however, is that the contacts between City Hall and the RGB were not only substantial, but also shocking, in that they show coordination and collaboration throughout the RGB’s process,” Mastro wrote in a letter to the judge. Text messages indicate that Mitchell and Sindhwani spoke multiple times over the phone between February and April. In addition to scheduling hearing dates, they also discussed key RGB reports. “Sending my PIOC notes now – please take a look before we chat, if at all possible,” Sindhwani wrote before a call on April 3, referring to the RGB’s Price Index of Operating Costs report. The annual report provides information on rising costs for rent-stabilized apartments. Other reports allegedly discussed include the RGB’s Income and Expense Study and the Mayor’s True Cost of Living Report. In an email, Sindhwani also requested that the RGB provide its agenda, timeline of reports and hearings, and underlying data for Deputy Mayor for Housing and Planning Leila Bozorg’s understanding of the process. “This was a particularly curious request because Bozorg was already very familiar with the RGB’s reports since, immediat
